after: ## How do positivists and interpretivists study society? (1.1)
alt: Positivist and interpretivist approaches compared on view, aim, model, data, what they value and their weakness. Durkheim’s Suicide (1897) is the classic positivist study; interpretivists reply that suicide statistics depend on how officials interpret deaths.
caption: Positivists seek reliable patterns and causes; interpretivists seek valid meanings.

after: ## How do positivists and interpretivists study society? (1.1)
alt: Two panels. Correlation: poverty and low exam results are found together, shown with a dashed link. Causation: an arrow from poverty to low exam results with a question mark, because a correlation alone does not prove one causes the other.
caption: Finding two things together does not prove one causes the other.

alt: Left: triangulation, a questionnaire followed by interviews with some respondents to cross-check findings. Right: a longitudinal study following the same group over time, as in the British birth cohort studies; it shows change but is expensive and people drop out (attrition).
caption: Triangulation cross-checks findings; longitudinal studies follow the same people over time.

after: ## What are the stages in research design? (1.3.1)
alt: Seven numbered stages: selection of topic, aims, hypothesis, target population, methods, operationalisation (such as measuring social class by occupation) and a pilot study to test questions and procedures.
caption: Research design runs from choosing a topic to piloting the questions.

after: ## How do sociologists choose a sample? (1.3.2)
alt: A sampling frame is the list; a technique is how people are picked from it. Five rows of twenty dots show each technique: random picks by chance, systematic picks every fourth, stratified keeps the same mix of groups as the population, snowball follows a chain of recruits, and quota fills set numbers with the first people found.
caption: Each technique picks people from the list in a different way, with different risks of bias.

after: ## Which primary methods can be used? (1.3.3 and 1.3.4)
alt: Questionnaires use open, closed, multiple-choice and scaled questions. Interviews range from structured with fixed questions to unstructured and conversational, plus group interviews. Observations are participant or non-participant and overt or covert, giving four combinations.
caption: Each primary method comes in types: know which type you would use and why.

alt: Three groups of issues. Theoretical: the researcher’s positivist or interpretivist perspective. Practical: access, response rate, funding and time. Ethical: informed consent, privacy and confidentiality, deception, prevention of harm and legality. Covert observation raises deception and consent issues; young people need parental consent.
caption: Check every research plan for theoretical, practical and ethical issues.
